Who can manage the activity list? d.ganzha Jira Product Management AI Mcp Server Agile Work Activity Types in Time Tracking: Dev, Review, Defects d.ganzha 9 min read · Oct 15, 2026 -- Listen Share Logging every hour as generic “work” gives you a total and nothing else. How to set up work activity types for time tracking and group reports by them. Press enter or click to view image in full size Work activity types in time tracking are the categories attached to each logged hour — development, code review, bug fixing, meetings — and in Sprintly Cloud an administrator defines them once, after which every time entry requires one. Without them a report can only say that the team burned 312 hours last week; with them it says that 118 of those hours went into review and defect fixing, which is the number a founder and a client actually argue about. This matters most for an outsourcing studio. A client who pays for a sprint does not ask “how many hours” — that is on the invoice. They ask what the hours were, and “Development” as a single line item is not an answer. The same question arrives from inside: if a third of the week goes into defects that shipped two sprints ago, that is worth knowing before the retrospective, not after the renewal. One bucket called “work” destroys the only interesting dimension Press enter or click to view image in full size Work activities: the categories that make a time report answer questions. The system already knows who logged an entry, on which issue, in which project, on which date — and therefore also the issue type, priority, status and assignee. All of that is derived; nobody types it. Exactly one dimension cannot be derived: what kind of work the hours were. Two hours on SPR-412 could be writing the feature, reviewing someone else's pull request for it, sitting in a call about it, or fixing the bug it caused. Same issue, same assignee, same day. Only the person logging knows which of the four it was, and the activity field is the one place to record it. Leave every entry on a single catch-all value and the loss is permanent. You cannot reconstruct the split from issue types, because a review of a Story is logged on the Story itself. The dimension is either captured at the moment of logging or it is gone. How to configure work activity types for time tracking Activities live in Administration → Issue Configuration → Activities , at /admin/activities . Reaching that screen requires the admin.access permission, which ships with the built-in Administrator role. Note for anyone planning delegation: activities have no dedicated entry in the permission matrix, so you cannot hand "manage activities" to a delivery lead without handing over admin access. The screen itself is deliberately thin. Each activity has a name and a flag, and that is the whole model: Create — click Add Activity , enter a Name (required), optionally tick Default activity , confirm. Default — only one activity holds the default at a time. Ticking the box on a second one moves the DEFAULT badge rather than adding another. Reorder — drag rows by the six-dot handle. List order is the dropdown order people see when logging time, so the activity picked twenty times a day belongs at the top. Rename — safe. Existing entries keep their reference and display under the new name, so a naming cleanup does not rewrite history. Delete — avoid it. Deleting a category that entries point at orphans those entries and makes attribution hard. The documented alternative is to rename it with a (retired) suffix and drag it to the bottom, which keeps old reports intact while steering new entries elsewhere. A fresh installation arrives with one seeded placeholder activity called All . It exists so the form is never empty, not because it is a sensible taxonomy — replace it the moment anyone starts reading time reports. The Activities guidance page suggests two to five meaningful categories such as Development, Code review, Testing and Design; that range is a good ceiling. The activity field is required, so the data is never partial On an issue, time is logged through Add time in the Time Tracking section. The inline form takes a duration, a date, an activity and an optional comment: Time spent 30m | 2h | 1d | 3w Date defaults to today, past dates allowed Activity dropdown, administrator-maintained Comment optional free text The activity dropdown is a required input, not an optional refinement — a small decision with a large consequence: there is no such thing as a half-categorised dataset. You never end up with most entries carrying a category and the rest not, every report hedged with a disclaimer. Either the hours exist and have a type, or they were not logged. The cost is that a badly chosen list becomes friction on every log. If the dropdown has fourteen entries and three plausibly describe the same work, people pick whichever is nearest the cursor — full coverage of meaningless data. Required fields punish long lists harder than optional ones do. Two mechanics matter before building a process on this. Entries are not editable, only deletable with a confirmation, and deletion recalculates totals immediately. And the sidebar totals — Time Spent, Estimate
